q: You want to call the yacht Blue Star. Which call is correctly built?
a: "Blue Star, Blue Star, this is Aurora, Aurora, OVER"
o: "Aurora, Aurora, Aurora, calling Blue Star, Blue Star, OVER"
"Blue Star, this is Aurora, please answer, OVER AND OUT"
"Hello Blue Star, it's Aurora here, do you read me? Over"
why: The station called first (once, twice if reception is poor), then THIS IS and your own name, then OVER.

q: You have finished talking to the marina and need no reply. How do you end your last transmission?
a: OUT
o: OVER AND OUT
OVER
OVER, STANDING BY
why: OVER asks for a reply, OUT ends the exchange; the two never go together.

q: You switch to 72 to call a friend and hear two other boats in the middle of a conversation. What do you do?
a: Wait until they finish, then make your call
o: Make your call at once — 72 is open to all
Break in with BREAK, BREAK and then call
Call your friend on 16 and stay there to talk
why: Always listen before you transmit and never talk over a conversation in progress.

q: From your berth you want to call the fuel dock, 200 m across the marina. The set is on 25 W. What do you do first?
a: Switch to low power, 1 W — it is plenty at this range
o: Leave it on 25 W, so they hear you clearly
Leave it on 25 W, but keep the call very short
Switch to dual watch so you hear their reply
why: In port use 1 W: it reaches the dock without blocking the channel for boats further away.

q: On 16 you hear: "Aurora, this is Blue Star, OVER" in reply to your call. What do you say next?
a: "Blue Star, this is Aurora, channel seven two, OVER"
o: "Blue Star, this is Aurora, we are anchoring tonight in…"
Nothing — just switch to 72 and wait for them there
"Blue Star, this is Aurora, channel seven zero, OVER"
why: Once contact is made on 16, propose an intership working channel and move there to talk.

q: Blue Star has agreed to move to 72. You switch over. What do you do there?
a: Listen a moment, then call: "Blue Star, this is Aurora, OVER"
o: Start your message at once without calling them
Wait in silence until Blue Star calls you first
Call "All stations, this is Aurora" so they find you
why: On the new channel, check it is free, then call the station again before your message.

q: You want a berth for tonight. How do you make the first call?
a: On the marina's channel: "Vega Marina, this is Aurora, OVER"
o: On 16, giving your whole request in one transmission
On 70 by voice, as marinas keep watch on it
On 72: "Any marina staff, this is Aurora, OVER"
why: Call a marina on its own working channel with a short call; the request follows once it answers.

fig.title: Arriving at Vega Marina
lines: Pilot book lists the marina's VHF channel
You are 1 mile off the entrance

q: You call the marina on its working channel and get no answer. What do you do?
a: Wait a few minutes before you call again
o: Call again straight away, a little louder
Keep calling every 15 seconds until they answer
Call them by voice on 70 to get attention
why: Leave a gap of a few minutes between calls; non-stop calling blocks the channel.

q: The marina answers your call. What do you say?
a: Your request in one short message: boat, length, nights
o: The whole story first, so they see why you need it
Nothing yet — wait for them to ask each detail
Your request on 16 instead, so others hear it too
why: Keep calls short and to the point so others can use the channel.

fig.title: Marina channel, a busy evening
lines: Marina: "Aurora, this is Vega Marina, OVER"

q: The marina asks you to pay in advance for the berth. Your crew starts to read the credit card number over the radio. What do you do?
a: Stop him — anyone listening can hear it; pay in the office
o: Let him, as long as he spells it phonetically
Let him, but switch to low power, 1 W, first
Let him, but on a duplex channel, which is private
why: VHF is open to everyone in range; never give card numbers or other private data on air.

q: You hear: "Aurora, Aurora, this is Blue Star, OVER". How do you answer?
a: "Blue Star, this is Aurora, OVER"
o: "Aurora here, go ahead, OVER AND OUT"
"This is Aurora, Aurora, Aurora, OUT"
"Blue Star, Blue Star, Aurora receiving"
why: Answer with the caller's name, THIS IS, your name and OVER.

q: You have just asked the marina whether they have a berth for a 12 m yacht. How do you end this transmission?
a: OVER — you are waiting for their answer
o: OUT — the marina will answer when ready
OVER AND OUT — to be extra clear
Just release the button and say nothing
why: End every transmission that needs a reply with OVER so the other station knows to speak.

q: You proposed 72 to Blue Star. They reply: "Aurora, this is Blue Star, seven seven, OVER". What do you do?
a: Reply "seven seven", switch to 77 and call them there
o: Insist on 72, since you proposed it first
Stay on 16 and talk there until you agree
Go to 72 anyway and wait for them there
why: The called station may propose another channel; agree it briefly and move.

q: At anchor, the children ask to play with the handheld and call each other on 16. What do you say?
a: No — 16 must be kept clear and the radio is not a toy
o: Yes, as long as the handheld is on low power
Yes, as long as each call is kept short
Yes, but on channel 70 rather than 16
why: Channel 16 must stay free for distress and calling; needless transmissions are not allowed.

q: The marina ends with: "…we will meet you at the fuel dock, OUT". What do you do?
a: Nothing more — the exchange is over; go back to watching 16
o: Reply "Vega Marina, this is Aurora, OUT"
Reply "Received, OVER" and wait for an answer
Reply "OVER AND OUT" to close it properly
why: OUT means the exchange is finished; no reply is expected.

q: Entering harbour, you hear: "Yacht entering harbour, this is Port Authority, state your name and intentions, OVER". How do you answer?
a: "Port Authority, this is Aurora, mooring at the town quay, OVER"
o: "Port Authority, this is Aurora, standing by, OUT"
"Received, Aurora entering harbour, OVER AND OUT"
"All stations, this is Aurora, mooring at the quay, OUT"
why: Answer the station that called you, give what it asked for and end with OVER.

q: Which line of this exchange breaks radio procedure?
a: Line 4
o: Line 1
Line 2
Line 3
why: OVER asks for a reply and OUT ends the exchange; "OVER AND OUT" contradicts itself.

fig.title: Your call to the marina
lines: 1 You: Vega Marina ×3, this is Aurora, OVER
2 Marina: Aurora, this is Vega Marina, OVER
3 You: a berth for one night, 12 m, OVER
4 You: thanks, see you soon, OVER AND OUT

q: What is the sensible next step?
a: Try again later, when you are closer to the marina
o: Keep calling every minute until someone answers
Send a PAN-PAN so the marina takes notice
Ask all stations on 16 to pass your request on
why: No reply at long range usually means out of range or busy; call again nearer, not more often.

fig.title: Calling ahead for a berth
lines: Marina 18 miles ahead, behind a cape
Two calls 10 minutes apart: no reply
Power 25 W, radio check fine this morning

q: In a crowded bay a motor yacht is dropping its anchor across your chain. You do not know its name. How do you call it?
a: "Motor yacht anchoring north of me in Vathi Bay, this is Aurora, OVER"
o: "All stations, all stations, this is Aurora, a boat is on my chain, OVER"
"PAN-PAN ×3, motor yacht in Vathi Bay, you are over my chain, OVER"
"Hello, the boat anchoring now, are you there? Aurora, OVER AND OUT"
why: If you do not know a vessel's name, identify it by type and position instead.

q: Blue Star agreed on 16 to move to 72. On 72 you call them twice, a minute apart, with no reply. What do you do?
a: Go back to 16 and call them once more
o: Keep calling on 72 every few seconds
Call them by voice on 70 instead
Wait on 72 in silence for an hour
why: If the other station does not appear on the working channel, return to where you last had contact.
